text: Three in the morning. An emergency room.
A doctor meets a very sick patient for the first time.
And her family has to have the hardest conversation of their lives, all over again.
That's where Sahara started. With five of us.
Basith and Awaiz run a small software company.
Dr Sujay and Dr Sharada are lung doctors, and Shirin is a medical student.
Back in August, Dr Sujay told us: patients say what they want, and none of it gets written down.
So we did what engineers do. We built everything.
Syringe drivers. Spinal cord compression. Sedation protocols. Twenty tools in two days.
Then Shirin, our medical student, asked one question.
Why would a family install this?
She was right. We'd built it for us, not for them.
So we changed it, one switch at a time.
Doctor tools became an app for patients and families.
When we got shortlisted, Basith and Awaiz rebuilt it as a real Android app.
And the doctors kept pulling us back to one thing. The goals of care talk.
With everyone's consent, the doctor records the talk. Sahara writes out who said what, and ticks off Dr Sujay's thirteen topics as they come up.
At first, we let the app write the note. The doctors said no. The doctor leads.
So now nothing is final until the doctor reads it, edits it, and signs. Then the family signs too, and it locks.
And at home, between visits, families get real help.
Symptoms and pain, marked on a body map, with trends for the doctor.
Snap a prescription, and every dose gets a reminder.
Ask your reports a question, and see the line that answers it.
And we gathered over sixteen hundred palliative care centres, in every state, with where to find morphine.
And families don't talk in one language. So it listens in English, Hindi, Telugu, Urdu and Kannada, even mixed in one sentence.
Back to that emergency room. One scan of her card, and the doctor knows what she wanted.
Oh, wait. Late one night, it hit us.
We kept asking how the patient feels. Nobody was asking the daughter.
So caregivers get their own check too, and someone to call.
Three months. Almost six hundred commits. A survey of doctors and hospitals. And doctors who kept telling us no.
It's live on Google Play today.
Sahara. Care that follows what matters to the patient.
